utterances.text: And, perhaps, if we limit this question even further, you had the opportunity during those meetings to see that the president of the Republic of Macedonia would sometimes give orders, direct orders that pertained to the security issues in the country at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And some of those orders or -- some of those orders which you personally witnessed being given by the president in relation to security matters were given directly to the Ministry of Interior, and even more specifically to the Minister, Mr. Boskoski; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And from those meetings which you had with the president, you also know that at the time, when Mr. Boskoski would receive such an order from the president, he would feel bound to obey such orders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine he would, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can turn your attention to another one of your investigator's note, Mr. Tucker, that would be at tab 74 of your binder. This is Rule 65 ter 369. Mr. Tucker, we haven't seen this particular document yet, I believe, but you remember you indicated to Mr. Saxon in your evidence in chief that you attended a number of meetings that pertain more specifically to the Neprosteno exhumation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall this particular note to be the record of one of these particular meetings? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps, for the transcript, I will go through briefly through the document for you. The purpose of this document or the purpose of this meeting was a meeting arranged by the Macedonian authorities in connection with the exhumation project proposed for confidential site near the town of Tetovo. It took place on Saturday, the 10th of November, of 2001 at 1300 hours in the assembly hall of the parliamentary building. And present during that meetings were Mr. Trajkovski, President of the Republic of Macedonia; Mr. Boskoski, as Minister of the Interior; Goran Mitevski, Director of Public Security; Mr. Dzikov, Public Prosecutor; Professor Duma, Director of Forensic Pathological for the Republic of Macedonia; His Excellency Mr. Norberg, EUMM Ambassador to the Republic of Macedonia; Mr. LeRoy, special envoy to the EU; Brigadier-General Keerle of NATO; Mr. van der Stoel, special envoy of the OSCE; Mr. Klaus Voellers, special political representative for NATO; Dr. Peer Schwan, colonel and military assistant for NATO; Mr. Craig Jennes, head of OSCE in Macedonia; yourself, and other leading figures for NATO, OSCE, and EU. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the record which you made of that meeting is a record of discussions which took place between these particular people in relation to the foreseen or proposed investigation in the Neprosteno area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can turn your attention to the second page of that document -- sorry, the fourth page of that document, I'll ask to you focus on the second paragraph on that page. I would but ask you to confirm that the "he" in fact referred to President Trajkovski, if you can look at the previous page.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the record of the meeting records the following that: "Mr. Trajkovski," the president of the Republic of Macedonia, "ordered," this is highlighted, "ordered Mr. Boskoski to increase police patrols, to issue them armoured vehicles and body armour immediately, and for them," the police, "to commence operations in the area tomorrow." That Would be Sunday, the 11th of November of 2001. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then you record a particular statement made by the president, Mr. Trajkovski, addressed to Mr. Boskoski in those terms: Mr. Minister, you will issue the police with all their powers now, and stated,'I'm the president of this country and that is that.'" Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you will recall a number of follow-up meetings to this particular meeting with the president Trajkovski and Mr. Boskoski; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, in particular, I would like you to turn to the next tab in your binder. That would be tab number 75. It is it Rule 65 ter 1D639. And as you will see from the record, Mr. Tucker, this is one of your investigator's notes, and it is -- it concerns a meeting, again pertaining to the Neprosteno exhumation process of the same day, but later in the day, on the 10th of November of 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And present at that meeting were Mr. Boskoski, Minister of the Interior; Mr. Mitevski, Director of ever public security; Mr. Dzikov as public prosecutor; Professor Duma, the Director of the Forensic Pathological for the Republic of Macedonia; His Excellency Mr. Norberg, the EU Ambassador to Macedonia; Mr. LeRoy, special envoy to the EU; James Pardew, the US special envoy; Brigadier-General Keerle of NATO; van der Stoel, special envoy for the OSCE; Mr. Klaus Voellers, senior political representative for NATO; Mr. Craig Jennes, head of the OSCE in Macedonia; Dr. Peer Schwan, military assistance to NATO; Mr. Szydlik, operation officer of the ICTY in Macedonia; yourself; and other unidentified leading figures from NATO, EU, and OSCE. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can look at the first page, Mr. Tucker, the first paragraph, unhighlighted paragraph, it says that the meeting was arranged at the incident insistence of the president; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to turn to the next page, and I ask you to focus on the fifth paragraph from the top. It starts with the word: "Mr. Boskoski." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. On page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, please, page 2.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There's a paragraph which starts with the words: "Mr. Boskoski referred to the meeting with the president and made several statements about the legality of the Macedonian government to conduct its affairs as it saw fit. He stated that he did not believe that anyone could guarantee 100 per cent security." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then if you can leap frog to the next paragraph, which starts with the word, "Mr. LeRoy." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. LeRoy is recorded as saying this: "Mr. LeRoy agreed that 100 per cent security could not be guaranteed. He also agreed that the operation should be begin as soon as possible. He also agreed that the suffering of the relative of the victims should be considered and that the president had the authority to proceed." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he said: "However, he did not agree that the operation should not be delayed for a short while to ensure the involvement of the international community as a whole. He felt that the delay for one or two days, a short time, would not make much difference." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can now turn to the next page, the third page of this record, you recorded Mr. Boskoski to say this: "Mr. Boskoski said that he agreed with what was said in principle, but he still -- but he stated that he still 'had in mind the instructions of the president. It was not possible for him to decide.'" Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And Mr. LeRoy is recorded as saying this: "He responded by asking that he, Mr. Boskoski, relay his request to the president immediately. He reiterated if there was delay of 24 hours, he would guarantee full cooperation and support." And then you made an annotation in parenthesis to the effect that: "In the mean time, a government aid had left the room to telephone President Georgievski." It should have been Trajkovski?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should have been, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you record the following: "There was some exchanges of view, some contradictory of the situation concerning the overall stability and security of the region. Mr. Mitevski explained that there had already been a delay of one week, and that should have been sufficient time for the international organisations to prepare." And then you made another annotation to the effect that: "The aid returned and spoke to Mr. Boskoski." And then you record Mr. Boskoski as saying the following: "The president has agreed to the meeting of the Crisis Management Centre for tomorrow at 9.00, Sunday, 11 November 2001; and he adds, although he does not believe that it is necessary." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, the cross-examination is now finished, and I would like to thank Mr. Tucker for his patience and assistance. The only things that would remain, Your Honour, would be the tendering of the a number of documents which have been used with Mr. Tucker during the cross-examination. The only question which I would have would be wether Your Honour would wish that we do so at this stage or whether you would wish for the sake of saving time that we do that at the end of the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may be clearer now, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, we would seek to tender what is under tab 26 of Your Honour's binder, which is Rule 65 ter 1D638, which is the transcript of the deferral hearing which related, in part, to this case and which has been used with the witness. The Defence would also move to tab 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, and 34 admitted. Those, Your Honour, are the investigator's notes of the 27 to the 29 of November of 2001, which were the subject of extensive cross-examination, and they were all prepared by Mr. Tucker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has an objection to the admission of one document. That is the document that is at tab 30. That's Rule 65 ter 1D657. The Prosecution understands this document solely to refer to matters related to the Tetovo regional court and the area under that court's jurisdiction and the Neprosteno exhumation site. And so, in the Prosecution's mind, there is no relevance of this document to the issues of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think, in response, that Mr. Saxon is correct, only in part. The document was believed to be relevant and when it was used in relation to two discrete issues. The first one, as Mr. Saxon pointed out is correct, was to the effect that it related to the Neprosteno investigation. It was used in the first place to demonstrate which authorities were competent within the Republic of Macedonia to investigate both the cases of Neprosteno and Ljuboten. The second issue in relation to which this document was used and the issue to which we believe is relevant is the issue of security or the lack thereof at the time, in particular as pertain to the sort of investigation and exhumation operation which were later the subject of a further set of meetings in Macedonia. So the two issue, in summary, Your Honour, are about the competent authorities to conduct such investigation and the issue of security in Macedonia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received along with the other documents you tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours document under tab 26, 65 ter 1D638, will become Exhibit 1D213. Document under tab 28 has already MFI'd and will become now Exhibit 1D195. Document under tab 29 has already MFI'd and will now become Exhibit 1D196. Document under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Document under tab 30, 65 ter 1D657, will become Exhibit 1D214. Tab 31 has already been MFI'd and will now become Exhibit 1D197. Tab 32, 65 ter 1D143, will become Exhibit 1D215. Tab 33, 65 ter 1D614, will become Exhibit 1D216. Tab 34, 65 ter 1D615, will become Exhibit 1D217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document would be under tab 37 of your binder, and that is the Trial Chamber decisions in relation to the request by the Prosecution for the deferral of five cases, including Ljuboten case, and this is dated the 4th of October of 2002. The document is publicly available, Your Honour. The reason why the Defence is seeking to tender this in these proceedings is that, formally, it is it not part of the record of this trial, since it proceeded the time of the indictment in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit 1D218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The next document, Your Honour, which we seek to tender is under tab 38 of the first binder. It is a so-called conclusion of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Macedonia concerning the deferral of the five cases in question to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, including the case of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The next two documents, Your Honour, are again investigator's notes prepared by Mr. Tucker in relation to preparation made for the exhumation in Ljuboten. They are at tab 49 and 50 respectively of Your Honours' binder, and they record two meetings of the 7th of March of 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document under tab 49 will become Exhibit 1D220, and document under tab 50 will become Exhibit 1D221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is -- the next document would be at tab 73 of Your Honour's binder. This is a document that wasn't used directly with this witness; although, his evidence was relevant to the particular point. In light of the response of the witness and in particular in relation -- in view of the fact that he has indicated the time-frame of his involvement in this case, there was no need to tender this document. This document, Your Honour, is the report in effect that was ordered or requested by the Office of the Prosecutor for a ballistic analysis of the ballistic material collected in Ljuboten. We've had a set of questions to Mr. Tucker in relation to this matter. I haven't used the report itself, but this a proposed exhibit by the Prosecution, Rule 65 ter 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that would be all. And I'm very grateful to you, Mr. Tucker. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I fully support the intervention interrogation of my colleague, Mr. Mettraux, and I will have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber continues to be appreciative of the cooperation between Defence counsel in the matter of cross-examination, which is important to the time taken with a witness. Thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, just to clarify a few points. As a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, you began working in Macedonia in November 2001.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And your work was directed not only towards the investigation of the events in Ljuboten but also toward alleged crimes committed by the NLA in other parts of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as we saw during the cross-examination, as part of your role, you participated in a number of meetings with representatives of the Macedonian government, starting in November 2001. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, if I can refer to you, or if I can refer to your position, at that time in Macedonia, as a member of the international community, for lack of a better label, you were not the only member of the international community who was present at those meetings with Macedonian authorities, were you?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Often, those meetings would be attended also by representatives of the OSCE, the EUMM, representatives of NATO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some of those meetings, were ambassadors from different countries also present, different nations?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, why did so many different institutions and nations offer assistance to the authorities of Macedonia with respect to these cases of alleged war crimes?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can simply answer that insofar as both these particular exhumations were considered to be crucial to the continuing stability in what was considered to be an uneasy, peaceful situation in Macedonia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, Mr. Tucker, was then Minister Boskoski present at some of these meetings during the Autumn of 2001 when you and other members of the international community were present?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now to what is now Exhibit 1D211. And, Mr. Tucker, this is at tab 74, so it is probably in the second binder that was given to you by my colleagues from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have that document in front of you, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This -- these are your investigator's notes from a meeting that occurred at 1300 hours on Saturday, the 10th of November, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the assembly hall of the parliament building. And present from the government of Macedonia, we see, was President Trajkovski; Minister Boskoski; Goran Mitevski; Stavre Dzikov, the public prosecutor; Professor Duma, the Director of Forensic Pathology for the Republic of Macedonia; and then we see a series of other people. We see His Excellency Mr. Norberg, who was the EU's ambassador to Macedonia; Mr. LeRoy, special envoy of the European Union; Brigadier-General Keerle, from the NATO Amber Fox Mission --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Mettraux on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were waiting for to you pause, Mr. Saxon. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I am grateful to you, Mr. Saxon, for pausing. Simply for the record, Your Honour, Mr. Saxon appears to have referred to the President Trajkovski as a member of the government of Macedonia. We believe he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if I stand corrected, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A nicety of constitutional law, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is a forte of Mr. Mettraux, so I am sure he is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see Mr. van der Stoel, special envoy for the OSCE; Mr. Kollers, senior political representative for NATO; Mr. Schwan, another NATO representative; Craig Jennes, the head of OSCE; yourself, Mr. Tucker; and then, in addition, other leading figures from NATO, the European Union, and the OSCE. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to the third page after that document, and I'd like to direct your attention, Mr. Tucker, to the second full paragraph on page 3, where Mr. LeRoy, the EU representative, states that, in his view, there was no requirement to rush ahead on the following Sunday; and, I believe, if I understand your notes, to rush ahead with the Neprosteno exhumation. Do you see that? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, and you are correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And Mr. LeRoy asked that some time be given to provide a more detailed plan, in order for the international observers to be able to properly prepare for the task. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then we see a paragraph that says this: "Mr. Boskoski strongly disagreed and gave various reasons for this. His main concern centred around the possibility of interference of the site by those intent on preventing the Macedonian authorities in establishing the truth and finding the remains of those missing." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph, we say that there were several heated exchanges taking place between the parties; although, President Trajkovski did not participate in those exchanges so far. And then we see that the Ministry of Interior's Director for Public Security, Mr. Goran Mitevski, commented that, if the authorities were to await political dialogue to run its course, they, Macedonia, would not move at all. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know it's been some years now since this meeting took place, but can you recall, Mr. Tucker, your impression, for lack of a better word, of what Minister Boskoski was pushing or promoting at that time? What was Mr. Boskoski trying to promote?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski wanted to move as quickly as possible to -- to commence the exhumation at Neprosteno. That was the fundamental point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is page 4 of the English version, and we see where, in the middle of the page, Mr. LeRoy agreed with the idea of an 8.00 p.m. meeting and attempted to go calm the situation. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say, "he attempted to calm the situation," are you referring to the atmosphere in that meeting or another situation?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The atmosphere in the meeting, sir. It became extremely heated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph, we see: "However, Mr. Boskoski adds some comments concerning the security issues involving Tetovo, and stated that he would send armoured vehicles and suitably protected police into Tetovo to counter the violence, shooting incidents," which in your opinion only added to the obvious annoyance of the president. You remark here on the obvious annoyance of the president; but as far as you can recall, did the president give any countermanding orders to Minister Boskoski, with respect to what Minister Boskoski said he was going to do in Tetovo?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, to my recollection, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph we see: "President Trajkovski, still agitated, stated to the audience: 'If you are doing this, trying to delay the exhumation deliberately, in order to extend your mandate, it will not work, because if I say to you that your mission is over by the 27th of November, then it will be.'" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When that meeting ended, Mr. Tucker, what was your impression then, at least related to these issues that were discussed at the meeting, which authorities would prevail, in terms of how these operations would be conducted and when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think it is a fair question to put to the witness to state what is impression were. What we would believe would a more useful question, and question which perhaps the witness could answer is: What, in fact, happened? And he could be referred for that purpose to the meeting later that day. But if he is asked to give his impression, I think it would be more assistance to the Chamber to know what version or what course, in fact, prevailed between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I can rephrase my question, Your Honour. I was focussing on the statement of President Trajkovski, saying that: "If I say to you that your mission is over by the 27th of November, then it will be." I'll try to ask my question a bit differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that moment, Mr. Tucker, did you have any doubts in your mind about the sovereign ability of the state of Macedonia to conduct its affairs as it saw fit?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no doubt at all who was in charge at that meeting .

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to what is in tab 75 of the binder in front of you, and this is now Exhibit 1D212.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see, Mr. Tucker, this is, again, some of your investigator's notes. It's notes that you made related to a meeting that took place later the same day at 2030 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, we see the list of who was present. This time President Trajkovski is not present. We see Ljube Boskoski; Mr. Mitevski; Stavre Dzikov, the public prosecutor; Professor Duma; and many of the same persons from the international community who were present in the earlier meeting, but now they were joined by Mr. James Pardew, who was a US special envoy, and we also that Mr. Szydlik, the operations officer from the ICTY field office in Skopje, was present. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can turn, please, to page 2 of these notes?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you look at the fourth full paragraph of these notes it begins: "Mr. Boskoski referred to the meeting." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This paragraph begins: "Mr. Boskoski referred to the meeting with the president and made several statements about the legality of the Macedonian government to conduct its affairs as it saw fit." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to what is the last page of this document, page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you on the last page, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's a paragraph at the start of that page, and it reads this -- it reads thus: "Howard Tucker addressed the 'chair'," and chair is in quotation marks. Mr. Tucker, who did you consider to be "the chair" of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski, Minister Boskoski, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you consider Minister Boskoski to be the chair of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was called at the direction of the president and was opened and resided over by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say it was "presided over by the minister," you're referring to Mr. Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Minister Boskoski, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was not presided over, for example, Stavre Dzikov?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After that first sentence, according to this note, you said -- you said that you did not believe that you had a function play in the meetings of Sunday, 11 November 2001, and then you said this: "Mr. Tucker suggested that with the permission of the Minister of the Interior, you would speak to Professor Duma to arrange a suitable time for a meeting on Sunday, 11 November, to discuss exhumation procedures." And then it says: "Minister Boskoski agreed with the suggestion." My question for you is this, Mr. Tucker: Why did you feel the need to seek the permission of the Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Minister of the Interior and, by association, the authorities of Macedonia were conducting the -- the investigation and exhumation process; and, as such, protocol dictated that I sought his permission to deviate from what was suggested; that is, the meeting of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Tucker, can you recall whether there were any additional meetings that you attended with members of the Macedonian authorities in which Ljube Boskoski was also present?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we've -- I have been shown several documents during the course of my cross-examination which shows Minister Boskoski as being present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, I -- all right. Let me put my question perhaps differently, then. During those meetings where Minister Boskoski was present with you and these other members of the international community, international institutions, did Minister Boskoski ever request that the ICTY, or the Office of the Prosecutor, or any other international institution provide assistance to the Ministry of Interior's own internal investigation into the events at Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During those meetings, did Minister Boskoski ever ask that the ICTY, or any other international institution, assist the Ministry of Interior to identify members of the Ministry of Interior who had been present in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would wish to object to this line of questioning. When we sought to ask, if you wish, the reverse questions, the reverse set of the questions about the collaboration of the Office of the Prosecutor towards the Macedonian authorities, Mr. Saxon objected repeatedly. Now we believe that Mr. Saxon is trying to ask the same set of question but putting the light, if I may uses that express, on the other side, and we were stopped from asking those questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what is at issue in this case is whether Minister Boskoski took reasonable and adequate measures to investigate the events in and around Ljuboten, and that is wholly relevant. That's why I'm asking -- that's why these questions are quite relevant. This is a materially different matter from questions about what the Office of the Prosecutor did. And, quite frankly, many, many questions about what the Office of the Prosecutor did or did not do were allowed by the Chamber. It was only one last series of questions that were disallowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During these meetings where you participated, Mr. Tucker, did Minister Boskoski ever ask that the ICTY, or any other international institution, assist the Ministry of Interior to identify members of the Ministry of Interior who had been present in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During those meetings, Mr. Tucker, did Minister Boskoski ever ask, ever request, that the ICTY, or any other international institution, assist the Ministry of Interior to identify which police officers might have committed acts of misconduct against ethnic Albanians detained at Ljuboten and subsequently gaoled at different police stations in the Skopje area?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will object, again, but this time on a different issue. If Mr. Saxon intends to ask Mr. Tucker about particular meetings, then I believe it would be Mr. Saxon to identify the meetings he is referring to. Mr. Tucker has made it clear, in his evidence in cross-examination, that the meetings in question, the eight meetings of the -- the eight meetings of the end of November of 2001, at none of those meetings which pertain to Neprosteno and Ljuboten investigation was Mr. Boskoski invited. And as Mr. Tucker explained, the invitations were at the request or the meetings were organised by the OTP, and the people invited were selected by the OTP. If Mr. Saxon has in mind a different meeting or a different set of meetings which pertain to the issue of Ljuboten, we believe that in the fairness and the accuracy of the record he should refer to the meetings in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution is referring to the two meetings that were attend the by Minister Boskoski, one of which he presided over on the 10th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, in that case, Your Honour, I have a further objection to it. Your Honour will recall that Mr. Saxon sought to have those two records of meetings excluded, or rather, not admitted on the basis that those meetings had to do with the Neprosteno investigation rather than the Ljuboten; in fact, those were solely relevant to the Neprosteno matter. To that extent, the line of questioning of Mr. Saxon is even less relevant, in our respectful submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the Prosecution's respectful submission, for whatever reason a meeting might have been called, that would not preclude a minister from raising a separate matter, Your Honour, particularly given who was present at those meetings. And I will also note that my objection to the admission of a document related to Neprosteno, in the Tetovo area, was denied. So, obviously, there is some relevance to this case from such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have had -- I have will to scroll back to the question. It got lost in the seesaw of submissions. But the question is particularly directed to Ljuboten and, therefore, the question is allowed, Mr. Saxon, if I have got the right question, page 75 line 7 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That would be the right question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I think, Mr. Mettraux, you have had a fair hearing on these points, so that will be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply, we would wish to know which meetings Mr. Saxon -- we understand the same question as Your Honour. We would only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has specified that. And if the answer, then, is nothing, because that didn't happen, that will be the answer. I think Mr. Tucker may now need reminding of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will ask my last question again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will even add a date to make sure that the record is clear. During the meetings on the 10th of November, 2001, Mr. Tucker, did Minister Boskoski ever ask that the ICTY, or any other international institution, assist the Ministry of Interior to identify which police officers might have committed acts of misconduct against ethnic Albanians detained at Ljuboten and gaoled at different police stations in the Skopje area, in August 2001?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During those meetings on the 10th of November, did Minister Boskoski ever request that the ICTY, or any other international institution, assist the Ministry of Interior to arrange meetings with relatives of the deceased victims of the events at Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During those meetings on the 10th of November, did Minister Boskoski ever ask that the ICTY, or any other international institution, assist the Ministry of Interior to arrange meetings with other persons, ethnic Albanians, who had been allegedly mistreated at Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001, or in nearby police stations?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, did any of the work performed by the ICTY and other international institutions in Macedonia, during the Autumn of 2001 and the first half of 2002, prevent the Ministry of Interior from carrying out its own internal investigation into the conduct of police officers in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will object to that. If Mr. Saxon has a particular matter in mind, I think it should be put to the witness, if -- so if only to identify whether this is an issue that comes from re-examination. There's a number of questions that were raised, and we would not object to those in particular as relating to the transmission of document, if that is the matter that Mr. Saxon has in mind. The sharing of information, I think, should be put clearly to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would not interfere with the form of question, Mr. Mettraux. That is the ultimate relevance of what has been a great range of detailed questions, many of which had been subject to considerable objection, and I'm speaking there of both cross-examination and re-examination. Continue, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you answer my last question, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you could repeat it for me, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Did any of the work performed by the ICTY and other international institutions in Macedonia, during the Autumn of 2001 and the first half of 2002, prevent the Ministry of Interior from carrying out its internal investigation into the conduct of police officers in and around Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please turn, Mr. Tucker, to what is at tab 27. So it is probably in the first binder that Defence counsel provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has probably been admitted, but it had Rule 65 ter 1D -- excuse me, it is an exhibit. It is Exhibit 1D35.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 27, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you may recall, Mr. Tucker, these are your investigator's notes pertaining to a meeting that took place at a quarter to 10.00 in the morning, on Tuesday the 27th of November, 2001, at the offices of the OSCE in Skopje. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And a number of representatives of the OSCE were present, as well as you and Mr. Milner and Mr. Szydlik. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you look, please, to the last full paragraph on page 1, your notes reflect Mr. Milner, who was deputy chief of investigations in the Office of the Prosecutor at that time, saying the following: "The ICTY would like to see the authorities," i.e., the Macedonian authorities "conduct their own investigation and conduct their own trials where appropriate." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "ICTY would evaluate the evidence and observe how the authorities deal with the issues; that is, Neprosteno and Ljuboten." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please now turn to what is tab 29, which I believe is now Exhibit 1D196. And these are your investigator's notes, Mr. Tucker, from a meeting at the offices of the Macedonian public prosecutor in Skopje, at 1505 hours, on Tuesday, the 27th of November, and we see that present at this meets was Mr. Stavre Dzikov, public prosecutor for Macedonia; one of his assistants, who is not named; an interpreter; and then yourself, Mr. Milner, and Mr. Szydlik?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you take a look in the second full paragraph, we see, again, some comments attributed to Dennis Milner, the department chief of investigations. And we see it says that Mr. Milner stated the reason for his visit was a follow-up to that of the Prosecutor, Ms. Del Ponte, and then it says: "He stressed the view of the Prosecutor that Macedonia was a sovereign state and had the responsibility and capability to investigate crimes of this nature," and then it continues: "He stated that it was not within the mandate of the Tribunal to interfere with that judicial process." Have you been following me, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to the next page, please, page 2. And, Mr. Tucker, if you look at the fourth full paragraph, there is a paragraph, and it is actually really just one sentence, beginning with the phrase: "Public prosecutor stated." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "The public prosecutor stated," and perhaps the word "that" is a grammatical error, "stated the willingness of the authorities to cooperate with the Tribunal..." -- no, I was wrong. I will start over. "The public prosecutor stated that the willingness of the authorities to cooperate with the Tribunal is at all levels of the administration, including ministerial, judicial, forensic, crime scene technicians (police), and the security forces." And one question that I had -- have for you, Mr. Tucker: When you wrote that note about that meeting, if you can recall, what did you understand what the word "cooperate" to mean, as the public prosecutor used that term. Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be open to the Tribunal at all levels, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And what does that mean, "to be open to the Tribunal"?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To assist us with any inquires that we have, to allow me as a monitor to participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn, please, to what is tab 28 of the binder. I believe this is now Exhibit 1D611. Mr. Tucker, this is one of your investigator's notes from a meeting on the 27th of November, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Saxon. I believe it is now an Exhibit 1D196 -- 195, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 1D195. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is your notes of a meeting at the Ministry of Justice in Skopje, and we see present was the then Minister of Justice for Macedonian, Ms. Mojsova; one of the Minister's assistants; Dennis Milner; yourself; Mr. Szydlik; and an interpreter. And we see, in the fourth paragraph on the first page, Dennis Milner explained that: "He would speak with the judiciary responsible for the Ljuboten investigation in order to establish what inquiries have been conducted to date, and any result that resulted from those inquiries." Do you see that, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to the next page, please, page 2. And on page 2, the Minister of the Justice is speaking in the first paragraph. And then in the second paragraph, the Minister of the Justice also stated that: "The authorities had agreed to provide whatever was required to conduct the investigations, ('manpower and other needs')." Mr. Tucker, whose investigation was the Ministry of Justice referring to, when he made this comment?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is referring to their, the Macedonian authority's, investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And according to this comment by the Minister of the justice, then, who was going to receive this "manpower and other needs" that was required?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The investigation team of whom or what institutions or government?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Macedonian institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fairness to the witness, I wonder whether the next paragraph should be put to him. It refers to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't see this as an issue of fairness to the witness, Your Honour. I'm not afraid to say this to the witness; but if the Chamber would prefer me to do this, can I do this. I don't see any issue of fairness to this witness, but I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We see no need, Mr. Saxon. Are you at a convenient point or are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Almost. Within a minute I think I will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, when you participated in these meetings with members of the Macedonian government authorities, the president, in November 2001, was the ICTY taking over any investigations from the Macedonian authorities at that time?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time - the end of November 2001 - was the ICTY taking primacy over, or taking charge of the formally investigative procedures being performed by Macedonian government institutions?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours. Can we please show the witness what is -- it is now exhibit 1D33. It is tab 41 A of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tucker, yesterday, starting at pages 5341 to 5342 of the transcript, there was a discussion about this particular document. And if you'll recall, this was the motion or proposal signed or submitted by the public security director of the Ministry of Interior, Goran Mitevski, on the 7th of September 2001. It was addressed to the public prosecutor's office and the investigative judge in Skopje, and it is a motion for the exhumation and autopsy of five persons who were apparently buried in Ljuboten village after the events of the 12th of August. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to page 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And near the bottom of page 2, there is a paragraph beginning on the 14th of August, 2001. Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that paragraph describes the fact that the Ministry of Interior was notified that five corpses had been found in the region of Ljuboten; an inspection team was set up, including an investigative judge and a deputy public prosecutor and officials from the Ministry of Interior; and they were going there to inspect the scene to identify the five corpses. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, at the bottom of page 2, we see that the inspection team attempted to carry out its assignment several times but was unsuccessful in doing so - we turning on to page 3- because representatives of the ethnic Albanians in Ljuboten used force to physically present them from accomplishing their task. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then, in the next paragraph, we see that the Ministry of Interior was continually monitored security situation in the village of Ljuboten and concluded that the objective condition did not exist for the inspection team to carry out their task in Ljuboten due to the security situation, due to the automatic weapons and sniper fire. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can now -- if you could turn, please, to what is tab 41, this Exhibit 1D34. You were also shown this document yesterday, Mr. Tucker. This is the Republic of Macedonia's, the Ministry of Interior's information about the events in the vicinity of the Skopje village Ljuboten from November 2001. And, Mr. Tucker, if you could, please, turn to the very last page, it says ERN number 1D00-1918. Are you on the last page now?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Take a look at the last full paragraph, and it says this is: "Having in consideration the importance of the exhumation as the investigative act, in order to resolve the reasons for their death, the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, immediately after the case, has submitted the written recommendation to the principal public prosecutor office, Skopje II, in Skopje, to start conducting the process of exhumation of the corpses of the people, in order to continue the post-mortem and thorough examination." Do you recall seeing this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall, and this is at page 5346 of the transcript, that you agreed with my colleague, Mr. Mettraux, that from the face of this document, it appears that the Ministry of Interior's proposal, that had been submitted by Mr. Mitevski that an exhumation be performed at Ljuboten, actually originated from Minister Boskoski himself. Do you recall that exchange with Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you turn now to tab 64, please, in that binder, and this is Exhibit 1D73. Mr. Tucker, as you may recall from yesterday, 1D73 is an Official Note, dated the 18th of September, 2001, that records a meeting that took place between Dragan Nikolovski, an investigative judge; Dr. Aleksej Duma, the head of the Forensic Institute; Dragoljub Cakic, a deputy public prosecutor; Mr. Besim Ramicevic, who was the head of the homicide department in the general crime sector of the Ministry of Interior; and Mr. Dzidrovski, the head of the identification department in the criminal technology sector. And you see from the first page that the discussion was about the possibility of affecting an exhumation and autopsy of persons who had died at Ljuboten. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn to the next page now, please, page 2. And after some more discussion, we see a sentence beginning with: "Furthermore." Do you see that, sort of in the middle of the page, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "Furthermore, in connection with the request, a security evaluation will be required on the possibility of conducting the operation." And then, in the last paragraph, we see that: "The investigative judge accepted our suggestion, and it will be realised accordingly, but then the investigative judge stated the need for another meeting in order to discuss things such as suggesting a time for conducting the investigation, in accordance with the security conditions on the ground." Do you see that, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we take from this document that the security conditions on the ground in Ljuboten were, can we say, at least still uncertain at this time, 18th of September 2002 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 18th of September 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 2001. Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, can you turn to tab 83, and this is Exhibit P55.10. Mr. Tucker, Exhibit P55.10 is a document dated the 18th of March, 2002. It was also shown to you yesterday. It was produced by the Department Public Prosecutor, Dragoljub Cakic, and you will see that in the end of the first paragraph Mr. Cakic says that: "It was impossible to do so. It was impossible to examine the bodies at Ljuboten on the 13th and 14th of August, 2001. Due to the known reasons, on-site inspection by the competent bodies was made impossible." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraph, it says: "Several activities have been undertaken on your part," and he is writing this to the investigative judge, "so as to perform the proposed investigation action. Until now, it was impossible to do so due to the same reasons. However, seeing as the situation in question is now changed, it is certain that the exhumation is to be performed soon." So can we cake from this, Mr. Cakic [sic], that up until the 18th of March, it was still impossible, due to the security situation in around Ljuboten village, to carry out the exhumation. Is that a fair reading?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say so, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if you allow me, let me just summarize what we've just seen. Sometime before the 7th of September 2001, Minister Boskoski makes a proposal to do an exhumation in Ljuboten village; and then that proposal was memorialised in the motion that was submitted by Goran Mitevski on the 7th of September, and that motion noted that such an exhumation was impossible, due to the security situation in Ljuboten. Are you with me so far?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then, at least until the 18th of March, 2002, it remained impossible to do an exhumation in Ljuboten village, due to the security situation. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, I think we will wait until we hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, how many years have you been a professional investigator?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including my time with the Tribunal, 32, 33 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, when someone proposes to you that you carry out an activity that is impossible, do you find such a proposal very helpful?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we will object at this time, and that was the object of our original objection. Mr. Saxon has summarized the motion, as he called the documents sent by Mr. Mitevski on the 7th of September, and said that the motion noted that such an exhumation was impossible, due to a security situation in Ljuboten. Mr. Saxon should be more precise, particularly in view of the question or the proposition as put to Mr. Tucker. The situation to which Mr. Mitevski referred to in the motion in question was the situation as the 14th of August 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I do stand corrected by Mr. Mettraux. What Mr. Mitevski stated was that: "As of the 14th of August, it was impossible, due to the security situation, to carry out an exhumation."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we saw that in September, the 18th of September, the security situation was still uncertain. Do you recall that, Mr. Tucker?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we also saw that up until the 18th of March, 2002 it was still impossible to do an exhumation in Ljuboten village. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So my question remains the same: When someone proposes to you that you carry out a activity that cannot be performed, do you find that a very helpful proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really do not wish to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Mettraux, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now we have allowed the question and the answer, Mr. Saxon. Do you think that there can be any useful comparison made between the situations facing this witness in his career and the situation posed here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. The comparison simply focuses on an impossible task, whether it was -- whether it was an impossible task -- a task that is impossible for this witness to have been performed 15 years ago when he was in the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We no need to go into lengthy submissions. We are attempting to point out to you, Mr. Saxon, that you are right on the edge on anything that might be of use in our of determination of the issues in this case, a question of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, if you can turn to what is tab 50, which will be in the second binder, please, this is 65 ter 1D663.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be Exhibit 1D221, if it assists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tab 50, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, yesterday, at pages 5366 to 5373 of the transcript, there was a discussion between yourself and Mr. Mettraux related to how ante-mortem information would be obtained from the families of the deceased in Ljuboten. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is a -- your investigative notes from a meeting at 1300 hours, on the 7th of March, 2002, with Mr. Cakic, the deputy public prosecutor; and a judge, Jani Nica; and the investigative judge, Dragan Nikolovski. And can you turn, please, there's a discussion here on the first page about security concerns for the exhumation, and then can you please turn to page 2. And you see in the second paragraph of page 2, we see that Dragoljub Cakic, the public prosecutor, raised the point that: "Even during peacetime, the Albanian community never consented to post-mortem examination of the dead, including instances of homicide. He queried the consent provided by the relatives of the deceased for such an operation to proceed now." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, yesterday, I believe you explained that: "Eventually, it was decided that the family members of the deceased would provide such information to the investigative judge on the premises of the OSCE." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did that actually occur? Was there a time or an event when relatives of the deceased came to the OSCE and the investigative judge was there and he took the necessary ante-mortem data? Did that actually occur?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it did, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I believe you mentioned yesterday that although that was an unusual event, it was within the law of Macedonia or it was not outside the law of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. It would require, I think, some special considerations by the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair, then, to say that in March of 2002, prior to the exhumations, even at that time with all of the ongoing inter-ethnic tensions, with respect to obtaining necessary ante-mortem information from the families of the deceased at Ljuboten, the Macedonian authorities were able to accomplish more than they could during peacetime, at least according to the opinion of Mr. Cakic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really apologise to interrupt once again, but the question, we believe, again, doesn't reflect the transcript. There was no suggestion that more was achieved at that but during peace time. What Mr. Cakic underlined is that during peace time as in during the crisis situation, the families, the Albanian families, sometimes refused to provided antemortem information. There is no indication on the record that they were not successful during peacetime to obtain this information. So the suggestion made by Mr. Saxon in his question that there would be an indication to the effect that they were being more successful than in peacetime, I believe, is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm clarifying a point or points that were raised on cross-examination, and I'm using this document which is a Defence exhibit to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could - and you will probably have to turn to the other binder, the first binder, Mr. Tucker - could you turn to what is tab 19, please. This is Exhibit 1D191.

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, this is the letter of agreement between the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY and the public prosecutor of Macedonia, which was shown to you during cross-examination, and I have some questions for you about this document. In the first paragraph, we see that Patrick Lopez-Terres, the chief of investigations, is writing to Mr. Dzikov that: "Further to previous meetings with representatives of the OTP, and verbal agreements made in relation to events at Ljuboten during 2001, I hereby document and present to you the conditions agreed for the progress of the relevant exhumations and subsequent judicial investigation process," and then we see a list of 14 so-called conditions. My question for you, first of all: These 14 conditions, they were conditions for who to do what?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the conditions agreed upon in order to facilitate the authorities of Macedonia to undertake the exhumation at Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was going to facilitate the authorities of Macedonia to undertake the exhumation with respect to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the assistance of myself as a mediator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And would it be fair, then, to say that, well, the Office of the Prosecutor through you was going to perform this facilitation?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So my question -- my next question then is: These conditions, whose participation or activities in the exhumation were these conditions referring to?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The authorities in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And why were these conditions important to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the -- the difficulties in commencing this operation evolved around various issues which have been highlight the through my examination and cross-examination, primarily the security conditions and the reluctance through mistrust of the relatives of the victims. So it was necessary to find -- to find and hopefully able to create a situation whereby all parties would be agreeable to the process of the exhumation and autopsies on the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the ICTY had not agreed to such conditions, or if agreement had not been reached between the ICTY and the Macedonian authorities on these 14 conditions, did anything prevent the Macedonian authorities from going forward with the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. At any point, then, could the Office of the Prosecutor control when or how the exhumation was going to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's not necessarily a simple question to answer, because as the role of a facilitator, as you put it just now, we, the OTP, that is, myself, would have to create a suitable date that was acceptable to all parties that were involved in this process, both the authorities in Macedonia, the relatives of the victims, and, of course, the international organisations that were participating, such as the OSCE and the NATO and EUMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I guess my question is, though: Who had the final word as to how and when the exhumation would be carried out?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Macedonian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you turn, please, to what is tab 10 in your binder, Mr. Tucker. You were shown this document during cross-examination, and you were asked whether you knew that the Ministry of Interior had sent the report of the -- actually, let me start earlier, Mr. Tucker. If you take a look at the document in tab 10, we see that it is a request for assistance, and it quotes part of the report of the first commission set up to investigate the events in Ljuboten. This was the commission that was established by Minister Boskoski in 2001, and we see a paragraph of that report quoted in this request. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know for a fact, Mr. Tucker, which Macedonian institution, or which individual in Macedonia, provided this information to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you turn, please, to tab 11 --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour. Perhaps, before we proceed, I would like to seek a clarification from Mr. Saxon as to whether they take issue with their own letter, which clearly states that the document was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by the Ministry of Interior. We understood that there was no issue taken since it is an official document of the Office of the Prosecutor. If the Prosecution, indeed, takes issue with that fact, we would seek to tender the letter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to what is tab 28 of the binder, Mr. Tucker, and this is Exhibit 1D195. And when you were shown this document, Mr. Tucker, and you were asked to comment about the comments of Dennis Milner, saying where Mr. Milner said in the fourth paragraph that "he would speak with the judiciary responsible for the Ljuboten investigation, in order to establish what inquiries had been conducted to date and any result of those inquiries," you said that: "The OTP's view was: Don't interfere with the judicial investigation." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now these notes were produced about a meeting of the 27th of November, 2001; and, of course, your work in Macedonia continued through the first part of 2002. My question is: This policy, do not interfere with the investigation of the Macedonian authorities, was that always the OTP's policy, as long as you were involved in this work?

utterances.speaker: HOWARD TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we've reached time. I don't know whether you're checking to see whether there is a last question; if not, we might continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have checked, and I don't believe there is a last question. I believe I have asked all the questions I need to ask. And, again, I'm grateful to Mr. Tucker for his patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you will be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber is grateful for your assistance, and you are, of course, now able to go back to your ordinary activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will now adjourn. We resume on Monday at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
